paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a syndromic neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures, and motor delay (Greene et al., 2024). Chen et al. (2024) described moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability in all affected individuals they studied. Most of these individuals were nonverbal and had dysmorphic facial features, and many had abnormal brain MRI findings and involvement of several organ systems. The disorder is caused by heterozygous, mostly de novo, variants in a small central region of RNU4-2. RNU4-2 encodes the U4 small nuclear RNA (snRNA) of the major spliceosome (Greene et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024).

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) analyzed Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms for 46 cases with RNU4-2 variants from the 100,000 Genomes Project (100KGP) who were annotated with the term 'neurodevelopmental abnormality.' Of these cases, 91% had intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay. These rates were broadly in line with term frequencies across intellectual disability cases in general. Compared with other neurodevelopmental cases, several terms were significantly overrepresented among the RNU4-2 cases: microcephaly in 57% (vs 18%), drooling in 13% (vs 1%), proportionate short stature in 28% (vs 7%), generalized hypotonia in 39% (vs 13%), seizures in 52% (vs 27%), and abnormality of the upper lip vermilion in 13% (vs 2%). No terms were significantly underrepresented.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypic information on 49 individuals (21 females and 28 males) with RNU4-2 variants. The median age at last evaluation was 10 years (range, 2 to 38 years). Forty-two had the n.64_65insT variant, 3 had other single-base insertions, and 4 had single-nucleotide variants (SNVs). All had moderate to severe global developmental delay (severe in 34 of 49) and intellectual disability (45 of 45). Of 36 individuals older than 5 years, 30 (83%) were ambulatory. Walking was achieved at an average age of 3.4 years (range, 17 months to 7.5 years), and some individuals had a wide-based or ataxic gait. Only 3 individuals had fluent speech. Of 45 with a speech abnormality, 35 were nonverbal and 10 had a few words. Other features were intrauterine growth restriction (8 of 45), short stature (37 of 49), microcephaly (37 of 48; congenital in 19 and acquired in 9), hypotonia (39 of 45), seizures (37 of 48), abnormal brain MRI (41 of 45), behavioral issues (30 of 45), autism spectrum disorder (21 of 44), sleep issues (15 of 32), hearing loss (10 of 46), and vision issues (38 of 48). The vision issues included optic nerve hypoplasia (8 of 37), strabismus (23 of 45), and nystagmus (18 of 40). Gastrointestinal features were constipation (29 of 44), gastroesophageal reflux (21 of 43), feeding difficulties (32 of 42), and gastrostomy tube placement (13 of 41).

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) reported dysmorphic facial features in 45 of 48 individuals. The features varied but consisted of a myopathic face with deep-set eyes (some widely spaced and some narrowly spaced), epicanthus, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares or underdeveloped alae nasi, large cupped ears (some posteriorly rotated), and full cheeks. They also included a distinctive mouth with full lips and downturned corners, a high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue. Seizure onset varied, with a median of 3 years and a range from the first year of life to 10 years of age. Seizure types included infantile spasms, focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, febrile seizures, and status epilepticus. The most frequent brain MRI findings were reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, delayed myelination, and other nonspecific white matter abnormalities. Involvement of several organ systems was reported for all individuals. Affected systems included vision (optic nerve hypoplasia, cortical blindness, strabismus, nystagmus), the gastrointestinal tract, and the skeleton (osteopenia, recurrent fractures, scoliosis, kyphosis, hip dysplasia). In fewer individuals, there were hearing, endocrine (hypothyroidism, growth hormone deficiency, pituitary abnormalities), limb, sleep, genitourinary, dental, cardiac, and cutaneous concerns. No significant differences in presentation were noted between males and females.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) found that most RNU4-2 variants in their cases had occurred de novo. One case had inherited the n.76C>T variant from an affected mother, and in another family the mother of a proband with the n.65A>G variant appeared to be mosaic. Chen et al. (2024) described the disorder as autosomal dominant, with heterozygous variants confirmed as de novo in 86 of 115 affected individuals. The parental allele of origin could be confidently determined in 54 individuals: 46 with n.64_65insT, 3 with other insertion variants, and 5 with SNVs. In all 54, the variant was on the maternal allele, in contrast to the well-established paternal bias of de novo small mutations. Chen et al. (2024) suggested that this might reflect negative selection in the male germline or imprinting. They found no association with maternal age for individuals with n.64_65insT.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) used whole-genome sequencing data from the 100KGP to compare the burden of rare variants in 41,132 noncoding genes between 5,529 unrelated intellectual disability cases and 46,401 unrelated controls. RNU4-2 showed an extremely strong dominant association with intellectual disability (posterior probability of association approximately 1, log Bayes factor = 55). All other noncoding genes had a posterior probability of association below 0.5. Three variants, observed in 34 intellectual disability cases, had a posterior probability of pathogenicity above 0.5. None of these 34 cases had previously been solved by a pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant. Eight additional participants outside the intellectual disability class carried one of these variants and had neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Five further variants nearby occurred only in affected participants. Together, the variants formed 2 contiguous regions, n.62-70 and n.73-79, in which no unaffected participant had a rare variant; these regions lay within a locus markedly depleted of variation in gnomAD. Of the 47 cases with a rare allele in these regions, the variant was de novo in 37 and of unknown inheritance in 10. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, occurred de novo in 33 different families. Fifteen individuals had SNVs, 10 of them confirmed de novo, and all had phenotypes consistent with those of individuals with insertions. These SNVs clustered at the 2 ends of the critical region. paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region (nucleotides 62-79) is loaded into the active site of the BRR2 helicase, encoded by SNRNP200, which unwinds the U4/U6 duplex during spliceosome activation. The n.64_65insT variant lies within the T-loop ('quasi pseudoknot'), and n.77_78insT lies in the region that base-pairs with U6 in stem III. Both regions are thought to stabilize U4/U6 pairing and to position the U6 ACAGAGA sequence to receive the 5-prime splice site. The authors performed RNA sequencing of blood from 5 GEL individuals: 3 with n.64_65insT, 1 with n.77_78insT, and 1 with n.78A>C. These individuals showed increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites (mean 8.8 events, compared with 0.7 in both unmatched and matched controls). Twelve abnormal splicing events were shared by 2 or more affected individuals and were absent from all 378 controls; 11 of the 12 involved increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites. Positions +3, +4, and +5 of the 5-prime splice sites pair with the U6 ACAGAGA sequence. At the sites with increased use, these positions shifted away from consensus, which the authors considered functional evidence that the variants disrupt accurate splice-site recognition during spliceosome activation. Chen et al. (2024) also showed that RNU4-2 is expressed at consistently higher levels than its homolog RNU4-1 in the developing human prefrontal cortex, with greater chromatin accessibility around RNU4-2. They concluded that RNU4-2 is the main U4 transcript in the brain.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) identified the heterozygous n.64_65insT variant (GRCh38 chr12:120291839:T:TA) in 89 of 115 (77.4%) individuals with NDD who had variants in the RNU4-2 critical region. In GEL, the variant arose de novo in 38 trio probands, and in 8 additional probands the detectable inheritance was consistent with de novo occurrence. It was absent from 3,408 diagnosed NDD probands, 21,817 non-NDD probands, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and All of Us, and was seen in a single UK Biobank individual. Sanger sequencing confirmed the variant in 8 individuals. In 46 carriers in whom it could be resolved, the variant was on the maternal allele. RNA sequencing of blood from 3 carriers contributed to the finding of increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites.
